title: Self-healing polymers from bio-based benzoxazine blended with poly (ethylene glycol) for anti-biofouling applications
abstract: Abstract Biofouling remains a significant challenge in marine industries, as conventional coatings often lose their anti-biofouling efficacy once they become damaged. Incorporating self-healing capabilities into antifouling coatings has therefore emerged as a promising strategy to extend service life and maintain long-term performance. In this study, self-healing polymers were developed based on a bio-based benzoxazine resin (E-fa), synthesized from renewable precursors including eugenol, furfurylamine and paraformaldehyde, and subsequently blended with poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG). The blends were formulated with varying weight ratios and PEG molecular weights. This work investigates the effects of PEG content and molecular weight on self-healing performance under thermal triggering, coating performance, water absorption, marine resistance, and antibacterial activity of the developed blended bio-derived E-fa/PEG polymer (P(E-fa/PEG)). The results indicated that coating performance (i.e., pencil hardness and adhesion) was found to be markedly affected by increasing PEG content, which is due to the flexible and hydrophilic nature of PEG. However, PEG incorporation significantly improved adhesion, increasing the adhesion grade from 1 A in neat bio-based polybenzoxazine (P(E-fa)) to 4 A in the blends, with no substantial differences observed across PEG molecular weights. The increase in PEG contents can enhance the self-healing efficiency of the P(E-fa/PEG) up to 86% healing, attributed to the increased chain mobility of PEG and the reversible reactions within the E-fa network. The P(E-fa/PEG) blends also exhibited excellent antibacterial performance, achieving up to 100% inhibition of  E. coli  and 73% inhibition of  S. aureus . Hence, self-healable E-fa/PEG polymer blends have been successfully developed in this work, with potential applications in marine antifouling coatings.
journal: Journal of King Saud University – Engineering Sciences

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Biofouling is a significant global issue for the marine industry and submerged structures, resulting in numerous adverse effects on both economics and the environment. Marine biofouling adversely affects vessel performance by increasing hull roughness, thereby reducing hydrodynamic efficiency and elevating fuel consumption, emissions, and operating costs. For mid-sized vessels of the United States Navy, annual maintenance costs are estimated at approximately USD 56 million, potentially accumulating to USD 1 billion over 15 years. Furthermore, biofouling contributes to ecological disruption by enabling the spread of non-native species across marine ecosystems (Galhenage et al.  13 ; Ghamarpoor and Ramezanzadeh  14 ). Biofouling is formed from the accumulation and growth of undesirable microorganisms, bacteria, algae, and marine organisms on the surfaces of submerged structures or equipment (Galhenage et al.  13 ; Nurioglu et al.  33 ). The formation of biofouling involves multiple stages; the first stage immediately occurs when the structure’s surfaces are immersed in the marine environment, and dissolved proteins or organic substances start to adhere to the surfaces within a minute. After that, the attached soft fouler, such as bacteria, diatoms, and algae, form a biofilm in this second stage, which facilitates hard fouler to settle, leading to the growth of hard fouler, including mussels and barnacles (Nurioglu et al.  33 ; Qiu et al.  38 ). Therefore, mitigation of these biofouling problems was considered by the development of effective anti-biofouling strategies, such as the conventional anti-biofouling approaches, like biocide-release, metallic biocide-release, and non-degradable polymeric coatings, which are used to combat biofouling (Leonardi and Ober  22 ). However, conventional coatings raise environmental and health risks due to their toxicity and limited long-term effectiveness. Due to limitations of conventional coatings, there is a growing interest in modern coatings, developing environmentally friendly, sustainable, and advanced coating materials (Galhenage et al.  13 ; Lu et al.  26 ). In practical applications, it has been observed that during transportation, unintentional mechanical damage—such as scratching and abrasion caused by pebbles or submerged debris—may occur. Such damage can substantially degrade the performance of the coating or lead to the exposure of the underlying substrate (Maan et al.  27 ). The mechanical damage might cause surface fouling and accelerate the functional failure of the coatings. One of the promising approaches to overcome this challenge is the introduction of the self-healing (SH) property into the antifouling coating (Asha et al.  6 ). Many research studies on the development of coatings with SH ability have been conducted, including grafted polymer coatings (Asha et al.  6 ), polymer composite coating (Cui et al.  11 ) and hydrogel (Li et al.  25 ).

Self-healing polymers (SHPs) are smart materials that can automatically or externally repair themselves via various stimuli, such as heat (Mora et al.  31 ), light (Amornkitbamrung et al.  3 ), or pH changing (Cong et al.  10 ). SH systems are divided into two categories: the first is an extrinsic system, which requires external healing agents contained in microcontainers (i.e., microcapsules, nanocapsules, or a vascular network) embedded in the polymer matrix (Veghari Atigh et al.  51 ). Due to the limitation in healing repeatability, which disables healing when the microcontainers are damaged. The intrinsic system, which does not require an external healing agent, can address these limitations because it relies on molecular interactions and reversible chemistry in polymer structures, allowing for an infinite number of healing cycles (Safaei et al.  41 ). More recently, significant researches have extensively explored the development of materials with SH ability for prolonging their shelf life and to heal micron cracks or damages with intrinsic mechanisms (Safaei et al.  41 ; Štirn et al.  47 ; Zhang et al.  57 ). One of the most effective mechanisms for achieving high healing efficiency is reversible covalent bonding (Amornkitbamrung et al.  3 ; Štirn et al.  47 ; Zhang et al.  57 ). Moreover, the SHPs using the reversible covalent bonding are introduced in various applications, for instance, soft robotics (Orozco et al.  34 ), e-skin sensor (Han et al.  15 ), and especially protective coating applications (Mora et al.  31 ).

Polybenzoxazines (PBZs) are a class of high-performance thermosetting polymers and have attracted the interest of numerous researchers for use in thermosetting smart materials, especially SHPs (Machado et al.  28 ; Urdl et al.  50 ). Several research studies of self-healing PBZ have been published, such as poly(propylene oxide)benzoxazine/diallybenzoxazine (Arslan et al.  5 ), poly(propylene oxide)-PBZ (Kiskan and Yagci  20 ) and poly(benzoxazine- co -urethane) (Sriharshitha et al.  45 ). However, the conventional benzoxazine resins are primarily derived from petroleum-based resources. Due to environmental issues and the rising energy crisis, consideration of renewable resources for the synthesis of bio-based benzoxazine resins has become interesting in polymeric materials (Leungpuangkaew et al.  23 ; Lu et al.  26 ). Many benzoxazine resins that use renewable resources have been studied, such as eugenol-furfurylamine-based benzoxazine (Mora et al.  31 ), vanillin-furfurylamine -based benzoxazine (Ruenpanya et al.  39 ) and renewable daidzein-furfurylamine-polyetheramine-based benzoxazine (Lu et al.  26 ). Among these bio-based benzoxazines, the eugenol-furfurylamine-based benzoxazine is an interesting system due to its functional group, which offers SH properties. Moreover, there are reported eugenol-furfurylamine-based compounds that can be antibacterial materials (Kowalewska and Majewska-Smolarek  21 ; Lu et al.  26 ). Nevertheless, the inherent brittleness of the PBZ due to its rigid structure, incorporating flexible or long-chain polymer networks, is an essential method to improve chain mobility and enhance the SH ability of SHPs (Wang and Xu  54 ). Therefore, the copolymerization or blending of PBZs with a flexible polymer is a promising approach to provide an appropriate molecular structure for use in SH applications.

Poly (ethylene glycol) (PEG) is a flexible, hydrophilic, non-toxic, and biocompatible thermoplastic polymer, which is formed from the ethylene glycol repeating units (Wang et al.  53 ). Due to the non-toxic and biocompatible properties of PEG, leading to its use in widely applications such as biomedical, food, pharmaceutical, and coating applications (Parray et al.  35 ). It has also been studied for copolymerization and blending with thermosetting polymers to enhance toughness and flexibility (Sajjad et al.  43 ,  42 ). Furthermore, PEG has interesting properties as being able to resist protein or bacterial adhesion due to its hydrophilicity, which can form a hydration layer on the surface of the coating, which is a preventing attachment mechanism, which is one of the coating strategies (Leonardi and Ober  22 ; Nurioglu et al.  33 ). PEG is commonly used in this antifouling coating strategy. There are several works on the antifouling coating that use PEG as a part of the strategy to combat antibiofouling organisms (Galhenage et al.  13 ). PEG not only enhances the toughness and flexibility of the thermosetting polymers but also is able to prevent bacterial attachment, which makes PEG an interesting material to use in this work. The novelty of this work lied in the integrated design of a multifunctional biofouling coating that combines self-healing effect, substrate adhesion, and anti-biofouling performance within a single polymer blend system. This approach was expected to improve coating durability after mechanical damage while maintaining resistance to biofouling, thereby offering a more practical and comprehensive strategy for the development of self-healing antifouling coatings.

Hence, this work focuses on developing self-healing polymers for use as coating in antibiofouling applications, which were prepared from bio-based benzoxazine, which are synthesized from the bio-based substances i.e., eugenol and furfurylamine, blended with poly (ethylene glycol). The influences of PEG molecular weights and contents on curing behavior, self-healing behavior triggered by heating, coating performance (pencil hardness and film adhesion), and antibacterial efficiency of the blended E-fa/PEG polymers were systematically investigated.

sections.heading: Materials
paragraphs: Eugenol (> 99.0%) and furfurylamine (98.0%) were purchased from Tokyo Chemical Industry Co., Ltd., United States. Paraformaldehyde (AR grade) and polyethylene glycol with a molecular weight of 1500 g mol-1 (PEG-1500) were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich Pte. Ltd., United States. Polyethylene glycol with molecular weights of 600 and 4000 g mol-1 (PEG-600 and PEG-4000) were purchased from Merck Co., Ltd. (Darmstadt, Germany). The synthetic seawater is as follows: ASTM D665 was purchased from Paragon Scientific Ltd. (Prenton, Wirral, United Kingdom). All chemicals were used as received and were not additionally purified.

sections.heading: Bio-based benzoxazine resin preparation
paragraphs: The E-fa resin was prepared from eugenol, furfurylamine, and paraformaldehyde in a molar ratio of 1:1:2 using a solvent-free synthesis approach (Ishida  17 ). The reactants were mixed and heated at 110 °C in an aluminum vessel for approximately 40–45 min until a homogeneous system was achieved. Upon cooling to ambient temperature, the resulting product appeared as a transparent yellow resin.
Scheme 1 Preparation of ( a ) E-fa resin and ( b ) blended bio-derived E-fa/PEG polymer

sections.heading: E-fa/PEG blended polymers preparation
paragraphs: E-fa/PEG blends were synthesized by combining E-fa with PEG of different molecular weights (PEG-600, PEG-1500, and PEG-4000). Initially, the E-fa resin was heated and stirred at 110 °C, after which PEG was incorporated at predetermined weight ratios (95/5, 90/10, 85/15, and 80/20). The resulting mixtures were continuously stirred to ensure homogeneity and subsequently cast into silicone molds. The samples were then subjected to a stepwise curing process in a forced-air oven at 130 °C, 150 °C, 170 °C, and 190 °C for 1 h at each temperature, followed by a final curing stage at 200 °C for 2 h. After curing, the specimens were allowed to cool to ambient temperature prior to further characterization.

sections.heading: Characterization and measurements
paragraphs: Fourier Transform Infrared (FTIR) spectra of the samples and confirmation of polymerization were obtained using a Spectrum GX, NIR FT-Raman spectrometer with a KBr mode (PerkinElmer, Inc., Shelton, CT, United States). The spectra were recorded in the range of 4000–400 cm − 1  with a spectral resolution of 4 cm − 1 , and 32 scans were captured.

Differential Scanning Calorimeter (DSC) (model DSC1 module from Mettler-Toledo (Thailand) Ltd., Bangkok, Thailand) was used to investigate the curing behavior and reversible reaction of the samples. An aluminum pan with a lid was used to contain a sample mass of 5–10 mg. To indicate the curing behavior, the sample was dynamically scanned from 25 °C to 300 °C, and to investigate the reversible reaction, the sample was scanned from 30 °C to 200 °C with a heating rate of 10 °C/min while nitrogen gas was purging at a rate of 50 ml/min.

Thermally triggering surface scratching is used to indicate the microscopic healing process of the samples. The samples were scratched using a scalpel blade, and then they were heated at 100 °C on a hot plate stirrer to activate the reversible reaction. The scratched surfaces of the samples before and after healing were investigated using the optical microscope (OM) in reflection mode (20X magnification, Nikon model ECLIPSE E600 POL from Nikon, Inc., Tokyo, Japan) with a Canon EOS Rebel T3 camera.

Dynamic mechanical analyzer (DMA) (model DMA1 module from Mettler-Toledo (Thailand) Ltd., Bangkok, Thailand) was used to indicate the macroscopic healing process of the samples. The rectangular samples were cut into two pieces, and the surfaces were touched immediately. After that, the samples were heated at 100 °C on a hot plate stirrer. The test was performed under tension mode, at a frequency of 1 Hz, a strain of 1 μm amplitude, and a heating rate of 1 °C/min from 20 °C to 60 °C under a nitrogen atmosphere. All samples were prepared into a dimension of 30 mm × 5 mm × 0.5 mm. The samples were investigated for storage modulus at the glassy state before and after healing to calculate the healing efficiency as shown in Eq. ( 1 ).
where Eʹ before  is the storage modulus at the glassy state of the samples before healing.
Eʹ after  is the storage modulus at the glassy state of the samples after healing.

Surface morphology of the poly (E-fa/PEG) fractured surface was examined using a field emission scanning electron microscope (FESEM; Quanta 250 FEG). Prior to SEM analysis, the fractured surface of all specimens was sputtered with a thin layer of gold and operated at an accelerated voltage of 5 kV. Fractured surfaces were captured at a magnification of 500x.

The adhesion of the samples was determined using the X-cut tape test method according to ASTM D3359-22. The hardness of the samples was evaluated using the pencil hardness tester (model QHQ-A) in accordance with ASTM D3363-22. The samples were coated on a SUS 304 stainless steel substrate with a thickness of 300 μm using a doctor blade coater.

Water uptake related to the water absorption of the film, which was determined according to ASTM D570. Three cured polymer specimens were weighed for the dry weight. The specimens were placed in a conditioner of both deionized and synthetic seawater. During the test, the temperature was 32 ± 2 °C. After that, the specimens were removed from the water, all surfaces were wiped off with a dry cloth, and the specimens were weighed immediately to collect the wet weight for every 1, 3, 5, 7, 15, 21, and 30 days. And then replaced in the water. Percentages of increase in weight during immersion, calculated as follows, Eq. ( 2 ).
where Dry weight is the weight of the specimen before immersion.
Wet weight is the weight of the specimen after immersion for each day.

The resistance of the coated samples was investigated in two liquids, deionized water and synthetic seawater. The coated samples were soaked in both liquids for 30 days. The physical appearance before and after testing of the coated samples, including the color of the liquids, was monitored to study the changes.

The water contact angles of the coated samples were measured using a contact angle meter (model DMe-210, Kyowa, Japan), under the standard conditions (50% relative humidity and 23 °C). Measurements were carried out with 1µL of the volume of water, and at room temperature. The water contact angles were measured and captured using FAMAS software with five repetitions at various portions of each sample.

The antibacterial efficiency of the neat P(E-fa) and P(E-fa/PEG) blends was assessed by examining the %reduction of both  Escherichia coli  ( E.coli ) and  Staphylococcus aureus  ( S.aureus ) bacteria on the polymer surfaces according to JIS Z 2801:2010. Each of the 30 × 40 mm specimens was placed into its own sterile petri dish. To get “Time 24”, incubation of all the Petri dishes at 37 ± 1 °C for 24 h and at not less than 90% relative humidity. These incubated specimens were placed into the sterile container, which contained a precise volume of neutralizer, and vigorously mixed to wash all the surviving bacteria off the surfaces into the neutralizer; thus, this liquid is a stock solution. The stock solution was diluted to a 10-fold dilution, and the appropriate dilutions were plated onto a standard agar medium and incubated until colonies were visible. sections.heading: Characterization and network formation of E-fa resin and E-fa/PEG blends
paragraphs: The molecular structures of the synthesized E-fa resin and its blends were analyzed using FTIR spectroscopy in KBr mode. As shown in Fig.  1 (a), the E-fa monomer exhibited characteristic absorption bands of the oxazine ring at 1229, 1150, 1013, and 940 cm − 1 , corresponding to asymmetric and symmetric C–O–C stretching, C–N–C symmetric stretching, and out-of-plane C–H bending vibrations, respectively (Mora et al.  30 ; Thirukumaran et al.  49 ). The methoxy-substituted benzene ring showed asymmetric and symmetric stretching vibrations at 1229 and 1013 cm − 1 . Peaks at 2927 and 2840 cm − 1  were assigned to C–H stretching of methylene groups in the oxazine ring and eugenol moiety. The presence of the allyl group was confirmed by absorption bands at 1634 and 913 cm − 1  (Amarnath et al.  2 ; Mora et al.  31 ; Thirukumaran et al.  49 ), while peaks at 1586 and 735 cm − 1  indicated the furan structure. The band at 1496 cm⁻¹ corresponded to a tetra-substituted benzene ring (Mora et al.  31 ; Thirukumaran et al.  48 ,  49 ). A weak, broad absorption around 3526 cm − 1  was attributed to O–H stretching of phenolic groups, likely arising from trace unreacted species due to the solventless synthesis without further purification (Amarnath et al.  2 ; Thirukumaran et al.  49 ). These spectral features collectively confirm the successful formation of the E-fa resin. Figure  1 (b) presents the FTIR spectrum of PEG-4000. A broad absorption at 3485 cm − 1  corresponds to O–H stretching of terminal hydroxyl groups. The symmetric C–H stretching vibration appeared at 2885 cm − 1 , while bending vibrations were observed at 1466 and 1343 cm − 1 . The characteristic C–O–C stretching vibration of PEG was identified at 1107 cm − 1  (Stern  46 ).
Fig. 1 FTIR spectra of ( a ) E-fa monomer, ( b ) PEG-4000, ( c ) E-fa/PEG mixture, ( d ) P(E-fa/PEG), and ( e ) P(E-fa)

The structure and network formation of the E-fa/PEG blend were also characterized using FTIR-KBr spectroscopy. The E-fa monomer was directly blended with PEG-4000, and the structure of the E-fa/PEG blend was investigated as shown in Fig.  1 (c). The spectrum exhibits the characteristic peaks of both E-fa monomer and PEG-4000, indicating the coexistence of both substances in this system. After stepwise curing at 130 °C, 150 °C, 170 °C, and 190 °C for 1 h at each temperature, followed by 200 °C for 2 h, the cured E-fa/PEG blend was obtained, as presented in Fig.  1 (d).

The disappearance of the characteristic absorption peaks of the oxazine ring at 940, 1013, and 1229 cm − 1  corresponding to the ring-opening polymerization of the benzoxazine monomer (Mora et al.  30 ; Thirukumaran et al.  49 ). The increase in the intensity of the absorption band between 3200 and 3580 cm − 1  was attributed to the formation of phenolic hydroxyl groups (Mora et al.  30 ). Furthermore, the absorbance peak around 1586 cm − 1  became broader after curing, which was associated with a substitution reaction occurring at the furan ring during polymerization, leading to an increase in the number of substituted furan rings in the polymer network (Mora et al.  31 ; Thirukumaran et al.  49 ). Moreover, the peaks at 1634 and 913 cm − 1  remained after polymerization, indicating the presence of unreacted allyl groups in the polymer structure, which could subsequently participate in self-healing via the Diels–Alder reaction. Additionally, when comparing the FTIR spectra of the cured E-fa/PEG blend with those of P(E-fa) (Fig.  1 (e) and PEG-4000 (Fig.  1 (b), no additional peaks were observed, suggesting that no covalent bonding occurred between E-fa and PEG, confirming that the blending was purely physical. These results collectively indicate that polymerization of E-fa proceeded successfully while preserving the allyl and conjugated diene functionalities required for the Diels–Alder-based self-healing mechanism.

sections.heading: Effect of PEG contents and molecular weights on curing behavior
paragraphs: The effect of PEG contents and molecular weights on the curing behavior of the benzoxazine monomer was investigated using differential scanning calorimetry (DSC). The summarized DSC data of E-fa monomer and E-fa/PEG blends were tabulated in Table  1 . Figure  2 (A)- 2 (B) illustrates the DSC thermograms of the E-fa monomer and E-fa/PEG4000 blends with various PEG contents. A sharp endothermic peak observed at around 74–84 °C was attributed to the melting of E-fa monomer, representing a solid-to-liquid state transition prior to polymerization. The melting temperature (T m ) of the E-fa/PEG-4000 blends was slightly higher than that of the neat E-fa monomer and tended to increase with increasing PEG content, shifting from 74 °C to 84 °C. This behavior can be attributed to hydrogen bonding interactions between the –OH groups of PEG and oxygen and nitrogen atoms within the oxazine ring, thereby requiring higher energy to disrupt these interactions (Chaiwichian et al.  9 ). However, the influence of PEG contents on the T m  was not pronounced (at approximately 82–84 °C). The T peak , which was the specific temperature at which the heat flow reaches its maximum value, refers to the temperature at which the fast reactivity of the polymerization reaction in the polymer system, corresponding to the ring-opening polymerization of the oxazine rings in benzoxazine, was clearly observed in both E-fa monomer and E-fa/PEG4000 blends. The T peak  values of E-fa/PEG-4000 blends showed no significant deviation from that of the neat E-fa monomer, and the enthalpy of reaction of the blends was observed to slightly decrease, indicating that the PEG incorporation did not significantly affect the E-fa curing behavior (Brown and Rider  8 ). Figure  2 (C)-(D) shows the DSC thermograms of 80/20 E-fa/PEG blends with various PEG molecular weights. The T m s of the E-fa/PEG blends were slightly higher than that of neat E-fa monomer and tended to increase with increasing PEG molecular weight, from 80 °C to 83 °C. This behavior was ascribed attributed to the enhanced intermolecular interaction arising from the longer PEG chain length, which required greater energy for melting (Chaiwichian et al.  9 ). In contrast, the T peak  of the E-fa/PEG blends decreased compared to that of neat E-fa but slightly increased with increasing PEG molecular weight. The decrease in T peak  for low molecular weight PEG might be attributed to the plasticizing effect and the higher concentration of hydroxyl group of PEG, which enhanced chain mobility and facilitates ring-opening polymerization. Conversely, higher molecular weight PEGs possess fewer hydroxyl end groups and tend to phase separate from E-fa matrix, thereby hindering diffusion and delaying polymerization, as reflected by the slight shift of T peak  to higher temperatures (Brown and Rider  8 ). To confirm complete E-fa curing, the cured sample was also evaluated by DSC, as presented with the DSC thermograms in Figs.  2 (B) and (D). The disappearance of the exothermic peaks indicated that the ring-opening polymerization was completed, which is consistent with the FTIR analysis.

sections.heading: Transition temperature of P(E-fa) and P(E-fa/PEG) blends
paragraphs: After stepwise curing, the P(E-fa/PEG) blends containing 15% and 20% PEG were excluded from further analysis because the samples could not be removed from the mold and failed to form solid specimens, remaining in a highly viscous, liquid-like state. Therefore, only the blends containing 5% and 10% PEG were subjected to subsequent performance evaluations. To investigate thermal transition behavior (state changing) of the neat P(E-fa) and P(E-fa/PEG) blends, differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) was performed, and the thermograms are presented in Fig.  3 . The DSC thermograms showed the glass transition of the P(E-fa/PEG) blends and neat P(E-fa) at around 50–60 °C. The glass transition might be included with the endothermic peak because of enthalpy relaxation due to the thermal history of the samples (Ebeid and Zakaria  12 ). For the P(E-fa/PEG) blends curves, the endothermic peaks were not exhibited clearly; this might be attributed to the incorporation of PEG. However, the addition of PEG led to a lower glass transition temperature compared to the neat P(E-fa) due to the flexibility of PEG, which facilitated the higher chain mobility and was generally associated with improved SH capabilities. Furthermore, both neat P(E-fa) and the P(E-fa/PEG) exhibited a broad endothermic transition starting at approximately 80 °C. This transition reflects the reversible transition in physical state between the rubbery state and liquid-like state of the neat P(E-fa) and P(E-fa/PEG), which can undergo a thermal-triggered reversible reaction (i.e., retro Diels-Alder reaction) to provide the SH capability, which allows the materials to repair damage. Therefore, the results implied that the reversible state changing of all the polymers can initially occur at 80 °C. This transition temperature is of critical importance for evaluating SH behaviors. A comparable reversible transition at approximately 90 °C has been previously reported for self-healing E-fa/ECO copolymers, attributed to the retro-Diels–Alder reaction, as described by Mora et al. (Mora et al.  31 ). Based on these observations, a temperature of 100 °C was selected in this work to ensure that the reversible phase change occurred while avoiding undesirable deformation of the P(E-fa/PEG) blends during SH processes. Furthermore, the small endothermic peaks around the temperature 100–170 °C that were observed in both neat P(E-fa) and P(E-fa/PEG) blends are attributed to the maximum state changing, which indicated the peak temperature at which the polymer undergoes a significant reversible physical change, influenced by its composition and directly related to the material’s network flexibility. The P(E-fa/PEG) blends exhibited a lower temperature than the neat P(E-fa), which is attributed to the increased flexibility of the polymer network facilitated by the flexible PEG.
Fig. 3 DSC thermogram of the neat P(E-fa) and P(E-fa/PEG) at ratios 95/5 and 90/10 with various PEG molecular weights

sections.heading: Self-healing behavior of neat P(E-fa) and P(E-fa/PEG) blends at various PEG contents and molecular weights
paragraphs: In this work, the self-healing behavior of polymer blends was mainly associated with the self-healing polymer phase, which corresponded to P(E-fa). The P(E-fa/PEG-1500) containing 10wt% PEG specimen was selected as a representative formulation to investigate the healing mechanism using FTIR spectroscopy equipped with a heating ATR accessory at room temperature (RT) (Fig.  4 i(a) and at healing temperature of 100 °C (Fig.  4 i(b). At both RT and 100 °C, the absorption bands of the polymer blend appeared at 1494 and 1586 cm − 1 , which were assigned to tetra-substituted arene and furan groups derived from polybenzoxazine (Ishida and Sanders  18 ; Mora et al.  29 ; Prasomsin et al.  37 ). As shown in Fig.  4 i(b), new absorption bands observed at 420 and 1545 cm − 1  were attributed to cyclohexene groups, whereas the band at 1333 cm − 1  was associated with the 2,5-dihydrofuran structure present in the polymer blends (Api et al.  4 ; Mostafalou and Mohammadi  32 ). In addition, the absorption peak at 1634 cm − 1 , corresponding to C = C bonds in the polymer blends, decreased in intensity (Hombunma et al.  16 ). This change was likely related to the reversible cycloaddition Diels–Alder reaction occurring during heating at 100 °C between furan groups and adjacent double bonds, resulting in the formation of cycloadduct structures within the polymer network (Wu et al.  55 ). These results agreed with previous studies (Mora et al.  31 ), which reported that the reversible reaction occurred in the P(E-fa) network and that P(E-fa) acted as the main healing component. Thus, the findings confirmed the important role of P(E-fa) in controlling the reversible reaction and self-healing behavior of the polymer blend system. Moreover, Fig.  4 ii presents the proposed healing mechanism through reversible cycloaddition reactions in P(E-fa/PEG). Overall, the results indicated that the reversible cycloaddition process at 100 °C contributed to the self-healing capability of P(E-fa/PEG).

The polymer blends were evaluated for microscopic self-healing using a thermally induced scratch method (Fig.  5 ). After scratching, the samples were heated at 100 °C for 5 min to activate the between the furan diene and allyl dienophile, forming cycloadducts that contribute to self-healing capability (Fig.  4 ii). The neat P(E-fa) exhibited splintered damage due to its inherent brittleness, and a similar fracture morphology was observed in the 5 wt% PEG blends. In contrast, the 10 wt% PEG blend showed smoother and sharper scratch features, reflecting reduced brittleness and increased flexibility (Runqing Ou,  40 ). After thermal treatment, neat P(E-fa) showed no observable healing, with the scratch remaining distinct. Conversely, PEG incorporation significantly enhanced scratch closure. Increasing PEG content from 5 to 10 wt% markedly improved healing performance, attributed to the thermoplastic nature of PEG, which enables viscous flow and damage filling above its melting temperature, thereby promoting chain mobility within the P(E-fa) matrix. The effect of PEG molecular weight was not clearly discernible. Macroscopic healing behavior was further assessed via a thermo-mechanical test. Rectangular specimens were cut, rejoined, and heated at 100 °C for 5 min without external pressure to simultaneously activate the Diels–Alder reaction and PEG-assisted flow (Fig.  6 ). The healing performance was quantified using dynamic mechanical analysis (DMA) by comparing the storage modulus at 20 °C before and after healing (Fig.  7 ), and the healing efficiency was calculated according to Eq. ( 1 ). Storage modulus was used to calculate the healing performance because it directly reflected the recovery of mechanical stiffness after damage and healing. For polymer coatings, the restoration of storage modulus indicated the reformation of the polymer network and the recovery of load-bearing ability. Therefore, this parameter provided a quantitative and reliable evaluation of the healing efficiency.

The results indicate that the storage modulus of P(E-fa/PEG) blends exceeds that of neat P(E-fa), which can be attributed to hydrogen bonding interactions between the phenolic hydroxyl groups of P(E-fa) and the terminal hydroxyl and ether oxygen groups of PEGs, as displayed in Fig.  4 ii. These interactions function as physical crosslinks, limiting chain mobility and enhancing stiffness. As the molecular weight of PEG increases, the storage modulus decreases due to the reduced density of hydroxyl groups, leading to weaker hydrogen bonding (Singh et al.  44 ). At higher PEG loadings, PEG acts as a soft segment within the polymer network, increasing chain flexibility and free volume, thereby further reducing the storage modulus; consequently, the 10% PEG blends exhibit lower modulus than the 5% PEG blends. In term of the healing performance, the P(E-fa) exhibited the healing effect with the healing performance of approximately 48% suggesting healing mechanism possibly occurred in P(E-fa) structure. When the 5% PEG was incorporated into the P(E-fa) at all molecular weight of PEG, the healing efficiencies were decreased to be 36–47%. This might be due to the decrease in amount of P(E-fa) which acted as healing agent in the blends system. In contrast, healing performance was improved with increasing PEG content up to 10% achieving 60–86%. This enhancement is attributed to flow-assisted healing facilitated by PEG (Runqing Ou,  40 ), together with increased free volume and chain mobility at higher PEG contents, consistent with microscopic observations showing near-complete disappearance of surface scratches.

sections.heading: Surface morphology of neat P(E-fa) and P(E-fa/PEG) blends at various PEG contents and molecular weights
paragraphs: The cross-sections of neat P(E-fa), PEG-1500, PEG-4000, and P(E-fa/PEG) blends were examined using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) to indicate specimen surface fracture, and the SEM images are shown in Fig.  8 . The results revealed that the neat P(E-fa) exhibited a smooth surface and a homogeneous fracture surface, indicating its brittle and highly cross-linked structure, which is characteristic of polybenzoxazine. Upon incorporation of PEG into the P(E-fa) matrix, the fracture becomes rougher, indicating the enhancement of toughness of the P(E-fa) due to the flexibility of the PEG. At 5% PEG of the blends, the fracture showed a slightly rougher surface compared to neat P(E-fa), which has an inherent brittle fracture. No obvious phase separation is observed, indicating good miscibility between the PEG and P(E-fa) matrix. The reason might be intermolecular hydrogen bonding between the ether group of PEG and the phenolic hydroxyl group of the P(E-fa) facilitate more compatibility of both components, and the results of the 10% PEG of the blends are similar to the 5% PEG of the blends. Therefore, the effect of PEG content slightly affects the miscibility of P(E-fa) and PEG at the molecular level. However, increasing the molecular weight of the PEG leads to more ductile fracture and slightly phase separation, as clearly observed in the P(E-fa/PEG-4000) blends due to longer PEG chains, leading to reduced chain mobility, hardly interpenetrate through the P(E-fa) matrix, and then slightly micro-phase separation occurs, while in the P(E-fa/PEG-600) and P(E-fa/PEG-1500) blends the small boundaries on the surface without phase separation are observed which attributed to the short PEG chains, easily penetrate P(E-fa) matrix, leading to well-dispersion at the molecular level, excluding the P(E-fa/PEG-1500) with 10% PEG that showed homogeneous surface without any boundaries on the surface, it might be indicated that it is the optimal formulation of this system. The results are along with the hardness and storage modulus results.

sections.heading: Coating performance of P(E-fa/PEG) blends at various PEG contents and molecular weights
paragraphs: The effects of PEG content and molecular weight on the coating performances of the P(E-fa/PEG) were systematically investigated in terms of the pencil hardness and adhesion, with the results tabulated in Table  2 . The water contact angle and surface free energy were also investigated to indicate the surface properties.

Table 2 Coating performance of the neat P(E-fa) and P(E-fa/PEG) blends Sample Thickness (µm) Pencil Hardness Adhesion The images of the after tape-testing P(E-fa) 300 2 H 1 A P(E-fa/PEG-600; 95/5) 300 2 H 3 A P(E-fa/PEG-600; 90/10) 300 B 3 A P(E-fa/PEG-1500; 95/5) 300 3 H 3 A P(E-fa/PEG-1500; 90/10) 300 HB 4 A P(E-fa/PEG-4000; 95/5) 300 2 H 3 A P(E-fa/PEG-4000; 90/10) 300 B 3 A

The pencil hardness test reflects the balance between surface hardness and flexibility of the coating films. The results demonstrated that variations in PEG molecular weight have a negligible influence on the hardness of P(E-fa/PEG) blends. In contrast, PEG content played a significant role, with hardness decreasing as PEG content increased. This trend was attributed to the intrinsic flexibility of PEG, which enhanced chain mobility and introduced a trade-off between hardness and flexibility. When considered together with storage modulus data, the results indicated a transition from a rigid, reinforced network to a more ductile and self-healable system. The 95:5 blends exhibit high stiffness and superior scratch resistance (2–3 H), primarily due to strong hydrogen-bonding interactions; however, such rigidity restricted chain mobility and limits self-healing efficiency (Singh et al.  44 ). Conversely, the 90:10 blends maintained higher stiffness than neat P(E-fa), as evidenced by their elevated storage modulus, but showed a notable reduction in surface hardness (2 H–B). These decreases reflected increased local chain mobility induced by the plasticizing effect of PEG, which facilitated viscoelastic flow and enhances self-healing performance.

Adhesion of coating films is governed by interfacial interactions with the substrate, which are strongly influenced by polarity compatibility. Material polarity can be inferred from hydrophilic–hydrophobic characteristics. As summarized in Table  2 , the adhesion of all P(E-fa/PEG) coatings on stainless steel improved from 1 A to 4 A with increasing PEG incorporation. This enhancement was attributed to the hydrophilic nature of PEG, which increased the overall polarity of the inherently hydrophobic benzoxazine matrix and promoted stronger interfacial interactions with the substrate (Galhenage et al.  13 ). Regarding PEG content and molecular weight, coatings containing 5 wt% PEG exhibited negligible differences in adhesion across molecular weights. In contrast, at 10 wt% PEG, adhesion improved from 3 A to 4 A as molecular weight increased from PEG-600 to PEG-1500, but decreased to 3 A for PEG-4000. This trend suggested that moderate molecular weight PEG enhanced interfacial compatibility through increased hydrophilicity, whereas higher molecular weight PEG introduced longer chains with relatively reduced effective polarity, leading to diminished adhesion.

The influence of PEG content and molecular weight on the surface properties of the coatings was evaluated through water contact angle (WCA) and surface free energy (SFE) measurements (Fig.  9 ). The results indicated that both parameters significantly governed the surface characteristics of P(E-fa/PEG) blends. Neat P(E-fa) exhibited hydrophobic behavior with a WCA of approximately 99°. Incorporation of PEG enhanced surface hydrophilicity, as reflected by decreased WCA and increased SFE, due to the presence of polar ether and hydroxyl groups. Increasing PEG content from 5 to 10 wt% led to a further reduction in WCA, suggesting improved wettability with higher hydrophilic segment incorporation. Regarding molecular weight, WCA decreased as PEG molecular weight increased from 600 to 1500, but increased at 4000, indicating an optimal hydrophilicity at PEG 1500. The reduced hydrophilicity at higher molecular weight might be attributed to restricted chain mobility within the rigid benzoxazine network and the lower density of terminal hydroxyl groups, limiting water interaction. Consequently, blends containing PEG 4000 exhibited relatively higher hydrophobicity (Abreu-Rejon et al.  1 ; Galhenage et al.  13 ). Surface characteristics are critical for anti-biofouling performance, which generally involves two mechanisms: antifouling (AF) and fouling-release (FR). Given the diversity of fouling organisms and their attachment mechanisms, combining these approaches is advantageous. Amphiphilic coatings, which integrate AF and FR functionalities, offer a promising strategy. SFE analysis using the Owens–Wendt method (based on water and diiodomethane contact angles) further confirmed this behavior. Neat P(E-fa) displayed an SFE of ~ 30 mN/m, characteristic of FR materials, whereas all P(E-fa/PEG) blends exhibited SFE values in the range of 33–43 mN/m. These intermediate values indicate amphiphilic surface properties, bridging the characteristics of AF and FR coatings (Pistone et al.  36 ).
Fig. 9 Water contact angle and surface free energy of the neat P(E-fa) and P(E-fa/PEG) blends

sections.heading: Water absorption and marine resistance of neat P(E-fa) and P(E-fa/PEG) blends at various PEG contents and molecular weights
paragraphs: The intended application of this work is marine antifouling coatings, where water uptake and resistance to marine environments are critical. Accordingly, water absorption was evaluated in deionized (DI) water and synthetic seawater at 32 ± 2 °C to assess practical performance. Neat P(E-fa) and P(E-fa/PEG) blends were immersed, and water uptake was monitored at 1, 3, 5, 7, 15, and 30 days, as illustrated in Figs.  10 a) and  10 b). The P(E-fa/PEG) blends exhibited higher water absorption than neat P(E-fa), reflecting the intrinsic hydrophobicity of P(E-fa) and the hydrophilic nature of PEG. Increasing PEG content led to greater water uptake in both media, attributed to the higher concentration of hydroxyl and ether groups capable of hydrogen bonding with water. Consequently, the 10 wt% PEG blends showed higher absorption than the 5 wt% blends, reaching approximately 30% in DI water and 18% in synthetic seawater after 30 days. At 5 wt% PEG, water absorption decreased with increasing PEG molecular weight, likely due to a reduced number of terminal hydroxyl groups and lower chain mobility (Kapanya et al.  19 ), which limited water interaction. In contrast, at 10 wt% PEG, water uptake slightly increased with molecular weight, possibly due to the greater abundance of ether linkages and the formation of larger hydrophilic domains, which enhanced water retention (Bolourchian et al.  7 ). The higher water absorption ability of the polymer blends could indicate more AF mechanism which is beneficial for antifouling coatings by formation a thin hydration layer, which works as a barrier and makes it difficult for biofouling or bacteria to attach.

In synthetic seawater, the influence of PEG molecular weight on water uptake was less significant, and overall absorption was lower than in deionized (DI) water. This behavior was attributed to the presence of ionic species (e.g., Na⁺, Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺), which interacted with the ether oxygen in PEG, forming ion–polymer complexes that shielded polar sites and suppressed hydrogen bonding with water (Yang et al.  56 ). The marine resistance of neat P(E-fa) and P(E-fa/PEG) blends was evaluated in DI water and synthetic seawater using films (300 μm) coated on stainless steel. The initial and post-immersion (30 days) appearances are presented in Fig.  11 . Prior to immersion, all cured films exhibited a typical black color of polybenzoxazine with smooth surfaces. From the results, in DI water, films containing 10 wt% PEG showed slightly rougher surfaces than neat P(E-fa) and 5 wt% PEG blends, likely due to increased hydrophilicity and water uptake. In contrast, films immersed in synthetic seawater exhibited largely similar surface morphologies, except for P(E-fa/PEG-4000, 10%), which showed pronounced roughness consistent with higher absorption. Overall, surface differences were less distinct in synthetic seawater, reflecting its lower water uptake compared to DI water. Additionally, small white deposits observed on film surfaces in synthetic seawater are likely due to salt residues. The results indicated that the following immersion, films were dried at 80 °C overnight to assess self-healing and coating performance. As shown in Figs.  11 (i) and  11 (ii) (row 3), cracking and delamination occurred, particularly in blends with 10 wt% PEG, indicating that excessive water uptake compromised structural integrity. Increased PEG content enhances water uptake and expands free volume into the surrounding medium. However, after 30 days, no significant color change was observed in either medium suggesting there is no noticeable leaching or dissolution of the specimen into DI water and synthetic seawater as shown in Fig.  12 . These findings indicated that the developed coating could absorb water and undergo swelling, which is beneficial for the AF mechanism, while maintaining its physical appearance without significant dissolution. Furthermore, the results also suggested that the P(E-fa/PEG) based coating could maintain the physical appearance after water immersion for 30 days that is a potential use for marine applications.

sections.heading: Antibacterial property of P(E-fa/PEG) blends at various PEG contents and molecular weights
paragraphs: Biofouling represents a major global challenge in marine environments, arising from the undesirable accumulation of microorganisms, including bacteria, algae, and other marine species, on submerged surfaces. The initial stage of biofouling involves the adsorption of biomolecules (e.g., proteins) followed by bacterial attachment; thus, preventing early bacterial colonization is critical for effective anti-biofouling strategies (Lu et al.  26 ). The antibacterial performance of neat P(E-fa) and P(E-fa/PEG) blends was evaluated using the JIS Z 2801:2010 standard by quantifying surviving colonies of test organisms. The antibacterial efficiencies against  Escherichia coli  and  Staphylococcus aureus  are presented in Fig.  13 , while representative colony images on nutrient agar after contact with the polymer samples are shown in Fig.  14 . The results indicated that all samples exhibited higher antibacterial activity against  E. coli  than  S. aureus , which can be attributed to differences in cell wall structure. Specifically, Gram-positive bacteria ( S. aureus ) possessed a thicker peptidoglycan layer that limits penetration, whereas Gram-negative bacteria ( E. coli ) contained an outer membrane rich in lipopolysaccharides (LPS), facilitating interaction with the hydrophobic E-fa component. This interaction disrupts membrane integrity and increases permeability (Kowalewska and Majewska-Smolarek  21 ; Lu et al.  26 ). Neat P(E-fa) exhibited moderate antibacterial activity, achieving 67% inhibition against  E. coli  and 28% against  S. aureus . Incorporation of PEG significantly enhanced antibacterial performance, with P(E-fa/PEG) blends achieving complete inhibition (100%) of  E. coli  and 72.6% inhibition of  S. aureus . This improvement was attributed to a synergistic mechanism combining (i) the intrinsic antibacterial functionality of E-fa, derived from phenolic and furan moieties (Kowalewska and Majewska-Smolarek  21 ; Lu et al.  26 ), and (ii) the anti-adhesive behavior of PEG, which formed a hydrated layer that inhibits protein and microbial attachment (Li et al.  24 ). Increasing PEG content further improved antibacterial efficiency; specifically, blends containing 10 wt% PEG outperformed those with 5 wt%. This enhancement was associated with the hydrophilicity of PEG, whose hydroxyl groups facilitated the formation of a hydration layer, while steric repulsion from PEG chains reduced bacterial adhesion (Galhenage et al.  13 ). Consequently, higher PEG content resulted in superior antibacterial performance. The effect of PEG molecular weight revealed that antibacterial efficiency increased from PEG-600 to PEG-1500 but decreased for PEG-4000. This trend was attributed to differences in chain length and hydrophilicity. PEG-600, with shorter chains, was likely more constrained within the polymer matrix, resulting in limited surface hydration. In contrast, PEG-1500 provided sufficient chain length and ethylene oxide units to enhance water binding and surface hydrophilicity, thereby improving antibacterial activity. However, PEG-4000, due to its higher molecular weight, tended to form more crystalline domains, reduced surface hydrophilicity and consequently diminished antibacterial performance, as reflected by increased water contact angle (Abreu-Rejon et al.  1 ; Galhenage et al.  13 ).

In addition, the surface characteristics, antibacterial effectiveness, and self-healing performance of the P(E-fa/PEG) coating were compared with those of other reported biofouling coatings as reported in Table  3 . The results showed that the developed coating exhibited amphiphilic surface behavior comparable to those of the reported coatings. However, it possessed a much higher modulus, indicating superior stiffness and durability for practical applications. Moreover, the coating demonstrated effective biofouling protection as well as self-healing capability, highlighting its potential as a durable multifunctional marine coating.

sections.heading: Repeated healing of P(E-fa/PEG) blend
paragraphs: From the overall results, they demonstrated that P(E-fa/PEG-1500) containing 10% PEG represented the most suitable formulation, providing an appropriate balance among self-healing performance, antibacterial effectiveness, and amphiphilic surface characteristics. The self-healing polymer specimen based on P(E-fa/PEG-1500) containing 10% PEG, after being immersed in synthetic seawater for 30 days, was further evaluated for repeated healing cycles. The specimen was scratched and subsequently heated at 100 °C for 5 min during each cycle. The effect of repeated healing cycles on the damaged width of the blend was also investigated, as presented in Fig.  15 . Based on the experimental results, the damaged width tended to increase as the number of healing cycles increased, suggesting that the healing performance decreased after repeated healing cycles. This reduction may be associated with heat accumulation and changes in the healing behavior of the polymer blend during repeated thermal exposure. However, the healing process did not appear to have a direct adverse effect on the coating adhesion, as no delamination or peeling of the coating from the substrate was observed throughout the experiment.

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: In this study, self-healing polymers were successfully developed by blending bio-based benzoxazine (E-fa) with poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) at various PEG contents and molecular weights for potential use in marine anti-biofouling applications. The effects of PEG content and molecular weight on curing behavior, self-healing capability, coating performance, water absorption, marine resistance, and antibacterial activity were systematically investigated. The results showed that PEG content had no significant influence on the curing behavior of E-fa, while molecular weight exerted only a minor effect. From healing performance results, PEG content could help improve self-healing ability of the polymer blends by facilitate polymer mobility. The blend containing 10 wt% PEG-1500 exhibited the highest healing efficiency of 86%, with nearly complete disappearance of surface scratches. In terms of coating performance, which is indicated by pencil hardness and tape test adhesion. the P(E-fa/PEG-1500) blends demonstrated superior properties. At 5 wt% PEG, the hardness reached 3 H, while at 10 wt% PEG, the hardness was HB, both the highest values among the tested films. In addition, the 10 wt% PEG-1500 blends achieved an adhesion grade of 4 A, representing the strongest interfacial adhesion in this study. Water absorption tests in both deionized water and synthetic seawater revealed maximum uptake values of 30% and 18%, respectively after immersion for 30 days, for the P(E-fa/PEG) blends and there is no significant dissolution occurred. The antibacterial efficiency showed that the P(E-fa/PEG) blends with 10%PEG have greater antibacterial efficiency than the 5%PEG blends, and the P(E-fa/PEG-1500) blend with 10 wt% PEG achieved complete (100%) inhibition of  E. coli  and 73% inhibition of  S. aureus . Moreover, all of the P(E-fa/PEG) blends possessed the amphiphilic surface characteristics, which are advantageous for fouling applications. Overall, the findings indicated that P(E-fa/PEG-1500) at 10%PEG is the optimal formulation for achieving a balanced combination of self-healing ability, antibacterial activity, and amphiphilic surface properties. The obtained self-healing polymer in this work exhibited a promising candidate as a smart material for potential use in marine anti-biofouling applications.
